title: Serious questions for Cambridge after professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns
description: The University of Cambridge is facing serious questions about its academic standards and push for diversity after its youngest black professor resigne
body: The University of Cambridge is facing serious questions about its academic standards and push for diversity after its youngest black professor resigned amid allegations of copying other academics' research.Jason Arday's appointment in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment. Now, Cambridge says it has launched an investigation after "new information" emerged about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments.There are two fundamental questions for the university.Did it fail to adequately check Arday's credentials when appointing him, and did it defend that decision because of an institutional push to position itself as more diverse?For one of the world's leading universities known for academic excellence and globally significant research, this is about its institutional culture and decision-making at the highest level.The biggest reputational risk surrounds the accusations of academic plagiarism now under investigation - and denied by Arday - because they get to the heart of what a university is about.The University of Cambridge uses the common definition of plagiarism as "passing off someone else's work as if it were your own without appropriate acknowledgement".There is no allegation more serious that can be levelled at an academic.One of the fundamental purposes of a research-led university is the creation of knowledge through original thinking, insights and inquiry.The quality of this is the foundation of Cambridge's reputation, and a source of significant funding.Arday did not start his university journey at an elite institution.He has a degree from the University of Surrey in education studies and physical education, a master's from St Mary's University in London, and a PhD in education awarded by Liverpool John Moores University.The reason the PhD has attracted so much attention is because it is the first major piece of original research anyone wanting a career as an academic must complete.Arday's critics claim that his work relied on copying other academics without properly crediting their work from the outset, which he denies.He went on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.In other words, there is a line of institutions behind Cambridge now facing similar questions about their appointment processes.The entire higher education system relies on accepting the qualifications awarded by another institution in good faith. Regulation and standards are meant to create a common currency.That has now unravelled with what began as a blog a couple of years ago escalating in recent weeks, with more journalists unpicking aspects of Arday's life story and asking questions.It is at this point Cambridge faces questions about whether it was defending its own reputation as much as an individual academic.Just a couple of weeks ago, the university was briefing journalists that this was a campaign against a black academic, its appointment system was rigorous, and it would be robustly defended.So why might Cambridge have had a blind spot that delayed an investigation which could settle the matter?The university has spent the last decade working to redress the perception that the institution is a bastion of affluent white privilege.Roger Mosey, the former master of the university's Selwyn College, said Arday's academic background was "unconventional" for a Cambridge professor, but that his life story as an autistic man who said he could not read until he was 18 was what had seemingly "made him a compelling candidate".Equality, diversity and inclusion are reasonable goals for a leading university, Mosey wrote in the Times, but risk becoming contentious "when they are baked into inflexible policies and questionable appointment processes".Part of the answer may also lie in how black academics feel in general as part of a tiny minority in the wider university community.In the last academic year, only 75 of Cambridge's 6,180 academics at all levels were identified as black, according to the Higher Education Statistics Authority (HESA).If you look at professors across the UK, 270 are identified as black out of a total of more than 26,000, according to HESA definitions - around 1%.The University and College Union has previously highlighted an ethnicity pay gap and called for it to be redressed. It declined to comment on this case.Both Cambridge and Oxford have faced sustained scrutiny over their whiteness as institutions, with vocal critics over the last 15 years including the MP David Lammy.He extracted data from the universities showing how few offers were made to black students despite the number being awarded top A-Level grades which would potentially qualify them for a place.In 2018, Cambridge said it needed help to attract more talented black students, and unexpectedly the rapper Stormzy answered the call by setting up a scholarship to encourage students to apply.Although the support was for a handful of students, it was a reputational coup for the university - allowing it to position itself as a more open and inclusive institution.Now it will have to balance the potential reputational fall out of the Jason Arday row for its academic credibility, with how that might be perceived by future talented black students and academics.

schema.headline: Serious questions for Cambridge after professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns

title: Trump again limits US birthright citizenship with new executive orders
description: Donald Trump is trying again to scale back birthright citizenship in the US, weeks after the Supreme Court shot down his previous attempt to eliminate
body: Donald Trump is trying again to scale back birthright citizenship in the US, weeks after the Supreme Court shot down his previous attempt to eliminate the right.The president signed two executive orders on Thursday, including one that expands the existing definitions of non-citizens whose children are not eligible for birthright citizenship.The second order bans so-called birth tourism, the practice of pregnant mothers coming to the US to give birth so that their babies will be citizens. "This should have happened years ago, but we're taking care of it now," Trump said from the Oval Office, criticising the Supreme Court's rejection of his previous bid to end the 150-year-old policy. "My Administration has guarded against the risks posed by malign foreign actors who attempt to swindle American citizens by taking advantage of the generosity of our Nation," the first executive order says.That order prohibits the automatic citizenship of babies born in the United States to two non-citizen parents where one of the parents is: a member of a foreign terrorist group, a foreign government employee, has attempted to gain citizenship through fraudulent means, or is living in US territories where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute.Birthright citizenship for people born in US territories such as Puerto Rico is codified by federal statute. Trump and members of his administration have repeatedly railed against birth tourism, including accusing Russian and Chinese adversaries of taking advantage of birthright citizenship to infiltrate the US. While announcing the executive orders from the Oval Office on Thursday, Trump said that hundreds of thousands of babies have been born through birth tourism in the US. The Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan research group, has said that the most expansive census-based estimate accounts for about 22,000 to 26,000 babies born in the US from birth tourism every year. Government data, according to the institute, showed that there were 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024."The idea (is) that people come here pretending to be a tourist, pretending to be a visitor," Stephen Miller, homeland security advisor and White House deputy chief of staff for policy, said while standing beside the president on Thursday."But the real reason they're here is to have a child, to make that child an automatic citizen, (to) leave our country and then have a US citizen child," he said, adding that those children then gain access to welfare benefits, the voting booth, and "all the other rights and privileges that belong solely to Americans".Miller said the president has the authority to ban birth tourism under a section of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which grants the president the power to set exceptions and limitations on who can enter into the country.On one of his first back days in office in 2025, Trump signed an executive order that tried to end birthright citizenship as guaranteed in the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution. A legal battle brought the case to the Supreme Court, which in June ruled that Trump's 2025 policies could not stand and birthright citizenship remained the law. The decision was a major blow to Trump's ongoing efforts to limit who can live, work, and become citizens in the US.The high court made "a bad decision, very unfair decision", Trump said from the Oval Office on Thursday while announcing the executive orders. "Our country suffers because of it, and we're ending in a different way."Gabriel Chin, a professor at the University of California Davis' School of Law, told the BBC that while parts of the order might hold up, other aspects "raise some serious constitutional questions".Chin said the president does have some power to restrict people coming into the US specifically for the purposes of having a child. "But once it does happen, once a child is born in the United States, I don't think the president has any power to decide that that child is not a citizen," he said, adding that the issue was settled in the Trump administration's recent loss in the Supreme Court. He called birth tourism a "drop in the bucket" against the millions of births in the US. "It's an unusual phenomenon," he said.

schema.headline: Trump again limits US birthright citizenship with new executive orders

title: Officer says he's 'appalled' PC Harper's killers could be released early
description: Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenc
body: Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, he said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case",  Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early."Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial."I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.PC Harper and Lissie had been married for just a month when he was killed in the line of duty.On Thursday, the police officer's widow said she "will not give up" and hoped people would share a petition calling for his killers to be denied early release from prison.She said: "Hopefully we can make the current government come to their senses and realise we cannot put people like this back on our streets."Justice should mean justice and serving the sentence given."The government said it was trying to avoid running out of prison spaces as soon as October this year.The justice secretary Alex Norris previously said about 1,000 prisoners would now not be released early following the revision to the scheme."If we drew it any wider we would have a prison capacity crisis," said Norris.Prisoners released on licence, he said, would be subject to "very significant controls on their lives" and victims would be consulted.

title: Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses
description: Image source, Stanford UniversityImage caption, Assistant professor Brian Hie, pictured on the left with a colleague, said of the work "this was new t
body: Image source, Stanford UniversityImage caption, Assistant professor Brian Hie, pictured on the left with a colleague, said of the work "this was new territory for us"ByHealth and science correspondentArtificial Intelligence has been used to design brand new viruses that are fully functional and can replicate in the laboratory, say US researchers.It is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI.The resulting 16 novel viruses were created to infect bacteria and pose no threat to people.The breakthrough has been labelled a "very significant turning point" in science that could unlock a new era for treating disease. But experts have also warned AI-designed viruses raise "urgent" safety and security concerns.AI tools are rapidly advancing and have already been used to design new antibiotics.But that is relatively simple compared with designing a new viable virus from scratch."This is a next step in the complexity that's designable by generative AI, this is the first time generative AI has been used to design a complete genome, it's something that can replicate and have other functions inside cells… this was new territory for us," Brian Hie, assistant professor at Stanford University, told the BBC.The technology works similarly to large language models, like ChatGPT, which predict sequences of text.In this instance the AI models, known as Evo1 and Evo2, predict the language of life rather than words.The AI models were trained on genetic codes from viruses, bacteria, plants and people.They were then refined to produce a type of virus, known as a bacteriophage, which infect only specific species of bacteria.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The AI models were trained on genetic codes from viruses, bacteria, plants and peopleThe Stanford researchers picked the most promising 302 AI designs and synthesised them in the lab. Of these, 16 proved effective at killing E. coli bacteria.Samuel King, a PhD student in the lab, said they realised the phage were working in the early hours of the morning. The phage were placed on petri dishes growing a layer of bacteria on them and the scientists waited for signs their new viruses were enjoying the feast."We were starting to see these clear spots and it was just extremely exciting," says King. When the results were shared with the wider team "the room spontaneously burst into applause", Hie recalls.Developing new phage could lead to new ways of treating infections that have become resistant to antibiotics.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Phage therapy is seen as a potential solution to the rising tide of bacterial infections that cannot be treated with antibioticsBut the breakthrough also points to the ability of AI to design new biology that goes beyond the natural world – what is known as synthetic biology.Hie argues this has the potential to "massively improve human health" by developing new drugs and therapies.But concerns have already been raised that the same technology could be used maliciously to create new diseases.In a commentary accompanying the publication in the journal Science, Dr Thomas Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke from the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University wrote that the findings raise "urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions".They said it was no longer a question of "whether generative viral genome design will exist" but whether it can be used without "enabling serious harm".For example, they said new viruses with the potential to cause disease "should not be pursued".The researchers themselves took steps to maximise safety. They excluded viruses that could infect complex organisms from the training database, performed the research on phage rather than viruses that infect people and it all took place in a secure laboratory.Hie argues even existing safeguards go a long way towards "ensuring that the technology is used for good".From computers bits to atomsViruses are not alive and it would take another significant leap for AI to generate living organisms.The genetic code of the phage is around 5,400 base pairs (letters) long. The smallest genome of a living cell is around 500,000 base pairs. The human genome is three billion base pairs.Hie says "it would probably be a lot of work, but not impossible" to attempt some simple organisms and they were "definitely interested in working towards" that.Prof Marc Güell, from the synthetic biology lab at Pompeu Fabra University in Spain, said the study was a "very significant turning point" because for the "first time in history, we are beginning to design biology on a computer".He said it "allows us to dream of exciting possibilities for tackling humanity's greatest challenges" such as developing phages to tackle disease, enzymes to treat genetic disorders and antibodies that could be used in immunotherapy.Prof Patrick Cai, chair of synthetic genomics at the Manchester Institute of Biotechnology, said the study was an "important milestone"."The significance extends far beyond phages – it suggests that genome language models are beginning to learn the design principles encoded by evolution, opening the door to AI-assisted genome writing."Image source, Stanford UniversityGet our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Tories to end social housing for foreigners' and 'Bottoms down'
description: A few of Friday's editorials reflect the anger about the government's early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales. The Daily Express, exte
body: A few of Friday's editorials reflect the anger about the government's early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales. The Daily Express, external calls on the prime minister to halt what it calls a "preposterous plan", which it says will reward sex offenders and the killers of police officers. The Sun calls Andy Burnham's failure to exempt two of PC Andrew Harper's killers from the scheme a "terrible decision", external.The Daily Mail and the Daily Telegraph lead on Conservative proposals to scrap social housing for many foreign nationals. The Mail calls it a "bold move", external. According to the Telegraph, the Tories believe the change will stop Britain from being treated as a "cash machine for the world", external. But it also highlights concerns from Labour about the effect on long-term UK residents, including "NHS staff".The Guardian, external says the government's review of youth unemployment will recommend that primary schools in England should identify children at risk of leaving education at 16 without a job. Alan Milburn, who is leading the review, tells the paper that "the warning signs are there from a very, early age".The Financial Times calls the sale of EasyJet, external to an American private equity firm the "latest foreign swoop". The paper says the £5.7bn-takeover paves the way for "another London listed company to be taken private", with the airline joining an "exodus from UK listings"."Number 10 aides show blokey Burnham the red card", declares the Times. It says Downing Street social media experts have told the prime minister to tone down his "blokeish", external videos - by limiting references to "football and the pub".Some of the papers poke fun at the suggestion drinkers could be discouraged from standing in pubs in London's West End. The Daily Mirror, external asks "wouldn't this effort be better spent making it a crime to leave when it's your round?" The Daily Star , externaldeclares it "madness", and pictures the band of the same name standing in a Soho pub.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Tories to end social housing for foreigners' and 'Bottoms down'

title: Canadian Open: Cameron Norrie saves match point to beat Alex de Minaur, Aryna Sabalenka through
description: Britain's Cameron Norrie saved a match point as he produced a superb fightback to beat world number seven Alex de Minaur at the Canadian Open.Norrie w
body: Britain's Cameron Norrie saved a match point as he produced a superb fightback to beat world number seven Alex de Minaur at the Canadian Open.Norrie was a set and 5-2 down against the Australian third seed before coming through 5-7 7-6 (7-5) 6-1 to reach the fourth round.De Minaur, leading by a double-break, had a match point on his own serve in the second set but double-faulted.He twice served for the match but, at 5-4 up, double-faulted again to put the set back on level terms.World number 37 Norrie edged the tie-break and then ran away with the deciding set to complete victory in two hours and 52 minutes."It was a great match to win and to test my level, and I can take so much confidence from this one," the 30-year-old said."The level was so high the first two sets. "From the beginning, [de Minaur] came out firing and I had to match it."Norrie - who reached the Los Cabos semi-finals last week - will face France's Arthur Fils for a place in the quarter-finals.De Minaur's exit means that fifth seed Ben Shelton is the only top-10 men's player remaining in Montreal.World number one Jannik Sinner and third-ranked Novak Djokovic withdrew before the tournament began, while top seed Alexander Zverev lost his first match.Sixth-ranked Daniil Medvedev, seventh seed Taylor Fritz and world number nine Flavio Cobolli also all lost in the second round.

schema.headline: Canadian Open: Cameron Norrie saves match point to beat Alex de Minaur, Aryna Sabalenka through

title: 162-year-old Guinness found off the English coast
description: Image source, Stefan PanisImage caption, When Stefan Panis found the bottle off the coast of DoverByAdam MandevilleBBC News NIHow far would you travel
body: Image source, Stefan PanisImage caption, When Stefan Panis found the bottle off the coast of DoverByAdam MandevilleBBC News NIHow far would you travel for a pint of Guinness? If the answer is to the bottom of the sea, you might be in luck.There's just one catch - the pint in question is 162 years old.When Belgian underwater photographer Stefan Panis discovered a bottle buried in a shipwreck off the coast of Dover in 2025, he had no idea what he had found. He just knew something about it had caught his eye.When Panis and his friend, Eddie Huzzey, surfaced, a quick rinse revealed the familiar Guinness branding. The bottle dates back to 1864."We lifted the artefact, and then on the surface a quick rinse revealed 'Guinness'," he said.Image source, Stefan PanisImage caption, The bottle of Guinness dates back to 1864Panis, who has been diving for more than 40 years, contacted Guinness to share the discovery.So far, he has recovered just one bottle, but believes many more remain buried beneath the sand surrounding the wreck and he already has plans to recover more when conditions allow."Seeing the size of the case, I think it is definitely a case of 24 bottles."But there might be more cases."Image source, Stefan PanisImage caption, Panis said he believes there are dozens more bottles in the shipwreckAfter the discovery, Panis' colleague Pawel Truszynski contacted a microbiologist specialising in beer at KU Leuven University in Belgium.Samples from the bottle have been sent for analysis, with researchers hoping to learn more about what the stout would have tasted like."There is always a chance that we can recover the complete DNA, and then we can do a small re-brew of the exact beer that was found in the 1860s," Panis said.If successful, researchers could recreate the taste of Guinness as it was brewed in 1864 using samples of the recovered stout.Image source, Stefan PanisImage caption, Panis has been diving for over 40 yearsBut there may be an even more intriguing possibility."There is a possibility that it's still drinkable. The question is if the sea water has come into the bottles through the corks."If not, most likely the beer would still be drinkable."And although Panis admitted he is "not that big" of a Guinness fan, he didn't hesitate when asked whether he would try the 162-year-old stout if experts declared it safe."Of course."'I would try it even though I don't like Guinness'Image caption, Fraser Hill (left), Katie Wilkinson, and Katie White (right) said they would try 162-year-old GuinnessFor some people in Belfast, the novelty of drinking a pint that's spent more than 160 years at the bottom of the sea was reason enough to give it a go.Fraser Hill, Katie Wilkinson and Katie White all said curiosity would outweigh any hesitation if they were offered a taste of the recovered Guinness."I would try it even though I don't even like Guinness," Katie White said.Image caption, Matt McCoppin and Natalia Nowacka agreed they would try the 162-year-old stoutOthers also needed very little convincing.Matt McCoppin said he would try the stout "in a heartbeat", while Natalia Nowacka admitted she would be nervous, but still couldn't resist the opportunity."I wouldn't know what to expect, I'd be quite scared," Natalia said.Noë Vernet also said the chance to taste such a historic drink was too good to miss."For the sheer experience, I would try it," he said.Image caption, Margaret Barr said she wouldn't try the GuinnessNot everyone was tempted, however.Margaret Barr said she would much rather enjoy a pint of Guinness fresh from the tap than one recovered from the seabed."Absolutely not," she said. "I'm a big Guinness drinker, I'm just not a risk taker."Image caption, Andrew Clarke said he would try the Guinness "halfway down me"Andrew Clarke, meanwhile, said safety advice would not keep him waiting.He joked the Guinness would be "halfway down me" before experts had the chance to declare whether it was safe to drink."I don't think it would age like a fine wine, but for the sake of mankind someone needs to drink it," he said."Maybe put a few more down there and see what happens 200 years from now."A spokesperson for Diageo said: "Discoveries like this provide a fascinating window into our past and help build a deeper understanding of our heritage. "Currently, our Guinness Archive team is liaising with the divers to gather more information and evaluate the find."

schema.headline: 162-year-old Guinness found off the English coast

title: Bruno Guimaraes: Jaissle not part of Newcastle captain's Arsenal decision
description: Newcastle United manager Matthias Jaissle says a decision about Bruno Guimaraes' future had already been taken by the time he first met the club's dep
body: Newcastle United manager Matthias Jaissle says a decision about Bruno Guimaraes' future had already been taken by the time he first met the club's departing captain.Arsenal are set to complete their protracted £75m move for the midfielder after a breakthrough in discussions.Jaissle briefly spoke to Guimaraes at the club's training camp in Spain earlier this week, but the 28-year-old went on to bid an emotional farewell to his team-mates and club staff."I met him quickly, but the decision was already made," Jaissle said in his first meeting with reporters following his appointment as head coach."It was a nice conversation. He's a fantastic player and a great human being. It's tough but for him now it's the next challenge and we need to deal with it at a later stage. "We trust the players who are here already, but we will also see some changes."Guimaraes is set to become the fourth key player to leave Newcastle in less than a year.Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali moved to Barcelona and Tottenham Hotspur respectively earlier in the window while Alexander Isak joined Liverpool last summer.Club legend Alan Shearer has sent Jaissle his "very best wishes", but previously warned it could be a "tough season" with some "very challenging times ahead" in a column for BBC Sport.Jaissle, though, sees the club's rebuild as an opportunity to start a new cycle and mould a young, hungry side after succeeding predecessor Eddie Howe."This is a challenge and there are so many transitions at the moment," he said. "Many big players left - legends of the club - but we need to see it as a chance."Not having too many excuses now, just thinking forward about what we can influence. "Control the controllables, I used to say, and I'm sure there will be progress this season."Jaissle has been focused on coaching the players currently at his disposal on the training pitches, but Newcastle are working on further additions before the start of the season.Newcastle have shifted policy this summer, targeting younger players on the Continent, with Lukas Hornicek the club's oldest arrival by a reasonable distance at 24 years of age.The club have spent around £146m to date on goalkeepers Hornicek and Ewen Jaouen, midfielders Aladji Bamba and Sean Steur and winger Bazoumana Toure.The quintet, like Jaissle, have never experienced life in the Premier League before.However, following trophy-laden spells in Saudi Arabia and Austria with Al-Ahli and RB Salzburg, the 38-year-old is relishing the challenge ahead."This is something I don't have on my CV, but that's normal in football," he said."At one point it has to be your first step and I'm now at that moment after being successful in Saudi Arabia and Austria. "Everyone was dreaming about being a part of the Premier League and now here we are."Newcastle start the new campaign against Liverpool at St James' Park on 23 August.

schema.headline: Bruno Guimaraes: Jaissle not part of Newcastle captain's Arsenal decision

title: Women's Super League: Mariona Caldentey says 2026-27 is Arsenal's time
description: Mariona Caldentey has won four Champions Leagues, six Spanish titles, six Spanish Cups, a European Championship and a World Cup - but her eyes light u
body: Mariona Caldentey has won four Champions Leagues, six Spanish titles, six Spanish Cups, a European Championship and a World Cup - but her eyes light up when discussing Arsenal's hopes of silverware in the upcoming 2026-27 season.With the Gunners chasing a first Women's Super League title since 2019, along with two domestic cups and another Champions League, she is explicit about what she expects."We have to do it - now it has to be our time."The last time Caldentey, 30, was spotted in an Arsenal shirt was in May, standing on an open-top bus as part of the men's and women's victory parade around north London.Hundreds of thousands of supporters lined the streets to celebrate a first Premier League title in 22 years for the men, with Caldentey and her team-mates also showing off the inaugural Women's Champions Cup they won against Brazilian side Corinthians in February.It was a prize to cherish last season but, having finished second in the WSL and had their Champions League defence ended by an 87th-minute Lyon winner in their semi-final second leg, the Spain midfielder wants to put things right this season."We need to take the next step and are ready for it," she said. "We need to be ambitious, have no fear and believe in ourselves."That does not mean we are going to win it - there are other things that we cannot control, but that's the message."We are professional athletes at a big club and we have to deal with pressure. We accept it and I think it's a cool part of the job."This summer, Slegers has strengthened her hand with seven new players, including full-back Ona Batlle, Caldentey's compatriot, and England dynamo Georgia Stanway to stiffen midfield.Caldentey says Arsenal came up short last season through inconsistency and hopes the signings will help overcome that hurdle."We have shown amazing moments and amazing games and others where we haven't been good enough," she said. "That happened too many times last year. It was painful."We have added a lot of quality and that will help us."With players such as two-time Ballon d'Or winner and fellow Spaniard Alexia Putellas arriving in the WSL, down the road at London City Lionesses, Caldentey accepts the league is getting tougher."It is a really attractive league," she said. "What you see and experience here, you don't get in other places. There are never any easy games."You want to play against the best - that's the challenge as a player and the quality here is really high."And any observer would count Caldentey as among the very best.In two seasons at Emirates Stadium, she has won WSL Player of the Season, come second in the 2024-25 Ballon d'Or and made the WSL Team of the Year both times.During that period, her role has evolved from forward to midfielder and yet, despite that, only Alessia Russo has scored and assisted more for Arsenal."You have to adapt to what the team needs," she said. "Last year, I played a different role, closer to our defensive line. I was not used to it but these things make you grow."I do things better now than a year ago. Of course I enjoy playing higher up where you can be more creative and more risky but whatever my coach or team needs, I'll do it."Her manager has stated clearly her team needs trophies. Caldentey is steeling herself to deliver.

schema.headline: Women's Super League: Mariona Caldentey says 2026-27 is Arsenal's time

title: Meta told to pay another $567m in New Mexico child safety lawsuit
description: A US judge in New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay another $567m (£421m) for its failure to warn the public about dangers its platforms posed to childre
body: A US judge in New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay another $567m (£421m) for its failure to warn the public about dangers its platforms posed to children, marking the largest against the company over child safety.Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the social media giant is a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution and that it must put the money in a fund aimed at reducing future harms.  Thursday's ruling is in addition to $375m in fines Meta was already ordered to pay in the case, for a total of $942m.Judge Biedscheid compared Meta to a factory, with advertising and content as its product and "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children to be the pollution that must be abated".A spokesman for Meta, which owns and operates Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and Threads, said Thursday: "We disagree with the ruling and will appeal.""We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts."Regarding the earlier $375m verdict in the case, Meta had said it intended to appeal the ruling and gave a similar explanation. It was the first time that a state had successfully sued Meta over child safety issues.Meta is currently facing thousands of lawsuits in the US over similar issues. In addition to the New Mexico rulings, Meta earlier this year lost a landmark case in Los Angeles which found it could be held liable for building addictive platforms.Bruce Daisley, a former European vice president of Twitter (now X), told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the New Mexico fine, while large, was "a drop in the ocean" for Meta.In its latest financial results, the social media giant posted $61bn in revenue from April to June - up 28% on the same period a year ago."But it's an indication that we are moving to a stage where social media is going to be tackled around the world," he said.Meanwhile, former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips told Today she believed US court challenges against big tech could enable the UK to take tougher action - without fearing it may damage UK-US diplomatic ties.The New Mexico case stems from a 2023 lawsuit brought by attorneys for the State of New Mexico, arguing Meta should be held liable for the way in which its platforms endangered children and exposed them to sexually explicit material and contact with sexual predators.In the first phase of the trial, Meta was found to have repeatedly violated New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act as its recommendation algorithms essentially "steered" young users toward harmful content and contacts.Recommendation algorithms are the tools that Meta uses to automatically curate the content a user sees on its platforms.In ruling on this second phase of the trial, Judge Biedscheid found that Meta's harms reached the level of "public nuisance", or an issue of health and safety that has become so widespread it is negatively impacting a general public.In addition to being the largest fine Meta has received over child safety issues, the ruling also appears to be the first time that a social media company has been deemed a public nuisance."Just as noxious pollution produced by the factory can harm the common public right to reasonably clean air, the harmful effects of Meta's platforms on children do not stay contained by its platforms and, instead, migrate to the internet as a whole and, perhaps most concerning, to the real world and create a common, societal burden on and harm to the affected children and their families and schools, as well as hospitals and law enforcement," the judge wrote.The fund that Meta has been ordered to create will be used to pay for efforts to mitigate "the wide-ranging impacts of the harm", Judge Biedscheid said.A vast majority of the money, totaling $420m, will go towards treatment of harms Meta's platforms have already caused, through the funding of "appropriate clinical or other behavioral health programs and professionals," according to the order.Another chunk of the money will go towards training around awareness and prevention, including for teachers and health professionals on how to deal with social media harms against children.The judge also ordered Meta to enact other measures, including ensuring that no account of a user under age 18 is recommended to an adult and that no adult can message an underage user, banning the sending or receiving of nudity by underage users and enacting a "1-strike policy for adult users who engage in child sexual exploitation."In addition, Meta was ordered to:Eliminate "like" counts for users under 18Ban push notifications for such users every day between 10:00 PM to 7:00 AM and to ban such notifications during the typical school year between  8:00 AM to 3:00 PM, except on weekendsImplement a mandatory usage limit for such users of 90 cumulative hours per month across Instagram and Facebook, or about three hours per dayNext week, another major trial against Meta begins in California. Nearly three dozen US states' attorneys general are suing the company for violating child privacy laws.

schema.headline: Meta told to pay another $567m in New Mexico child safety lawsuit

title: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?
description: ByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsDo you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more
body: ByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsDo you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more than 50 years and is still used by around half of all UK households.But it has struggled to thrive in recent years amid fierce competition from online giants like Amazon, with sales stagnating.  Its owner Sainsbury's recently announced it was selling the chain for a lot less than it paid for it just 10 years ago. But the new owners say they see "real opportunities" for growth, including opening new standalone shops. Can they succeed where Sainsbury's did not?Image caption, Enrico has fond memories of using Argos's now-discontinued print catalogue When the BBC spoke to shoppers in central London this week, the retailer seemed to divide opinion. Some, like Enrico, 28, said they loved the convenience of same-day collection, and felt nostalgic towards a brand which unlocked fond childhood memories."It was a great way of doing your Christmas shopping," he told the BBC. "We'd go into our local Argos and we'd get the massive print catalogue."Argos's encyclopedia-like catalogue was once dubbed "the laminated book of dreams", but the company stopped printing it in 2021.At one point it was Europe's most widely printed publication.Image source, Bloomberg/Getty ImagesImage caption, Many Britons have fond memories of the Argos catalogue, which the company stopped making in 2021Image source, Bloomberg/Getty ImagesFor others, though, Argos has not moved with the times and is at odds with the seemingly endless online choice. "I feel Amazon is a lot easier because it gets delivered straight to your door with Prime," said Emily, 22, adding that she only used Argos to buy appliances, not "day to day" items.Jack Cunningham, 26, from Kent often uses Argos to pick up things when he's at work in London.The scientist said the big draw was convenience: "If I need something in the moment and can't wait for delivery, normally I'll get it in Argos."You can order something really cheap on Amazon, and it might come and be the wrong size," he added.For years, commentators have asked whether Argos could build a business to take on Amazon, the biggest online seller in the UK.But while Argos has invested a lot in digital, it never quite happened. It made £4.1bn of sales last year, compared with £32bn for Amazon in the UK.'Remind people it exists'Image source, Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty ImagesImage caption, Argos has around 200 standalone shops, down from 845 in 2016 Argos does, however, offer something its online rivals don't - a large network of stores, concessions in Sainsbury's shops, and collection points that mean customers can click and collect on the same day, free of charge.Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth thinks Argos could capitalise on this, along with its reputation as a trusted British brand. However, she thinks it needs to improve its app so it can compete with online players like Amazon, Shein and Temu.  "I think if you asked people to name five High Street retailers, they wouldn't name Argos," she added. "It's almost about reminding people it exists."Figure caption, What do people want from Argos?Argos hasn't been front of mind for Georgia, 27, for ages. She thinks it is outdated and not for her. "It's very old school isn't it? I'm more of an Amazon shopper."Argos could also do better on customer service, thinks Hugh Radojev, editor of Retail Week.  "It's not an exciting place to shop, or what it used to be for kids around Christmas. Under a new ownership you'd hope they could get it back into the zeitgeist." Image caption, Nicole wants Argos to open more standalone shopsSince 2012, Argos has gone from having 845 standalone shops to around 200 - although it also has opened about 450 shop-within-shops in Sainsbury's stores. This was seen as a smart move, allowing Argos to tap into Sainsbury's large customer base. Argos will keep all of those concessions after the takeover, and customers will continue to get Nectar loyalty card points for all their purchases.But Nicole, 40, an Argos fan from South London, says she wants the chain to expand further."It would be nice if they could go in other supermarkets like Tesco," she added.'Argos has a history of being different'Argos's new owners have ruled out deals with rival supermarkets, but they do plan to forge other "partnerships" and open new standalone stores. The group, called Swift Partners, includes several seasoned retail veterans, one of them a former boss of Co-operative Group. Retail analyst Richard Hyman thinks this ownership will be a better fit than Sainsbury's, which was focused on selling food. But he is sceptical about how much Argos can grow in such a "tough retail market".Shuttleworth is more optimistic, saying with a "ruthless focus" Argos can thrive and even put Amazon under pressure."Argos completely revolutionised the way we shop when they came out and they have a history of being different," she said. "If I was marketing director I would be thinking about how to bottle that for 2027."Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.Get in touchHow will you be affected by the issues in this story? Share your experiences

schema.headline: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?

title: Gianni Infantino: Mexico defies Concacaf to join Argentina in supporting Fifa president
description: However, Conmebol did "express its concern about the repeated unilateral actions taken without resorting to dialogue or the institutional mechanisms p
body: However, Conmebol did "express its concern about the repeated unilateral actions taken without resorting to dialogue or the institutional mechanisms provided for dealing with this type of situation".Meanwhile, the football association of 2026 World Cup runners-up Argentina praised Infantino for recognising and apologising for his "errors".It described his decade-long tenure as Fifa president as "centred on the development of soccer worldwide and institutional strength based on a clear, stable, and transparent governance model".Infantino is unanimously backed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF), but faces opposition from European football's governing Uefa and Concacaf.European teams could still boycott the World Cup as Uefa said its conditions had not been met, despite Infantino's plan being aborted."Assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again," a Uefa statement read."These conditions have not been met."Uefa has already said it has lost confidence in Infantino, calling the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal a "shabby, back room, opaque deal".The English FA has sent a letter withdrawing its support for Infantino, while Wales, Albania and Croatia are among other individual associations to have turned their back on the 56-year-old.Concacaf described Infantino's proposal as "a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first", and that "this recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour".However, unlike Uefa, it did not go as far as to say it had lost confidence in the Fifa president. Before Infantino withdrew his proposal, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood "in solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf in opposition to the plans.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Mexico defies Concacaf to join Argentina in supporting Fifa president

title: Gianni Infantino: Uefa says Fifa's backing of its president 'changes nothing'
description: European teams could still boycott competitions including the World Cup as Uefa says Fifa's defence of its president Gianni Infantino "changes nothing
body: European teams could still boycott competitions including the World Cup as Uefa says Fifa's defence of its president Gianni Infantino "changes nothing".The English FA has sent a letter withdrawing its support for Infantino in reaction to the plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.European governing body Uefa said in a statement its conditions had not been met, despite Infantino's plan being aborted."First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and secondly," Uefa's statement said. "Assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again."These conditions have not been met."Uefa has already said it has lost confidence in Infantino, calling the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal a "shabby, back room, opaque deal".But on Thursday, Conmebol, the South American confederation, and the Confederation of African Football (Caf) backed Infantino, as did the football associations of World Cup co-hosts Mexico and tournament runners-up Argentina.Infantino had offered all associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups, through the FFE subsidiary.World governing body Fifa said during Wednesday's meeting "mistakes" regarding FFE were "acknowledged", saying it was "not the intention" for the Fifa Council and members association to "feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently".Uefa's statement in response added: "Uefa made it abundantly clear in its statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency. That position holds."Yesterday's announcement that some people employed by the Fifa president (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing."Fifa has been approached for comment.Infantino arrived at Fifa's offices in Rabat, Morocco on Wednesday in now-familiar fashion, chauffeured to the building in a motorcade, sitting in the back of a Mercedes with blacked out windows.Some questioned whether he would still be the Fifa president when he left.Yet if anything, on the surface at least, Infantino appears emboldened.This was not the 56-year-old being ordered to a hearing to explain his actions. It was Infantino who summoned members of the Fifa management board to sit around the table with him, to talk through the events of the last week.Secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, Infantino's right-hand man, had been critical in an internal memo to staff, calling the FFE proposals "a sad and reproachable series of events".After the meeting finished it appeared to be water under the bridge, with Infantino and Grafstrom pictured sat next to each other and smiling at a Women's Africa Cup of Nations match between Malawi and Zambia. If there were clear-the-air talks, they appear to have worked. Other members of the Fifa management board to attend the meeting included finance chief Thomas Peyer, legal chief Emilio Garcia Silvero, chief of staff Daniel O'Toole, chief of member associations Elkhan Mammadov and media relations director Bryan Swanson.BBC Sport has been told that Fifa's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, was not invited.Lamour strongly criticised Infantino's FFE plan, saying it was "the project of one person", and "the time has now come for football's political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions". He added: "I lose my job, then so be it. At least I'll sleep well tonight."Lamour has declined to comment to the BBC. Fifa has been approached for comment.What concerns Uefa is that this meeting was a gathering of employees who are themselves part of the regime. It is unknown if Infantino was forced to answer difficult questions about his plan. Questions such as: who was involved? Whether there was a competitive tender process? And if he stood to benefit personally? While Fifa said "mistakes made were acknowledged" and an "apology was made", there was no direct accountability for the controversy.Uefa still wants answers to those key questions and will not be content until it gets them - or Infantino leaves.Uefa is in something of a pickle as it tries to get rid of Infantino.The easiest route to success was the slow turning of the vice throughout this week, hoping to exert enough pressure to force him to quit.Yet the Swiss appears to have no intention of walking away.European football looks like an outlier, struggling to gain enough support to topple him. On Thursday, Lamin Kaba Bajo, the president of the Gambia Football Federation, praised Infantino's "courage" and for the U-turn, and said he was "willing to give him my support more than ever".Only Jordan, one of the few countries which did not back Infantino before last week, has publicly stated it will not vote for his re-election in March. Concacaf, which oversees football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, also issued a public statement after the proposal was aborted but, unlike Uefa, it did not go as far as to say it had lost confidence in the Fifa president. Conmebol said on Thursday it would not support "any action or procedure that disregards" Fifa's mechanisms before the presidential election. Similarly, the Mexican Football Federation shared a statement to X expressing their support for Infantino, saying it would not recognise or approve any process convened outside of Fifa's institutional framework. The Argentine Football Association also published a letter in support of Infantino and the Fifa board, which it said had provided "institutional solidity" with its current "stable and transparent" business model.Caf said its executive committee "unanimously reconfirmed" its support for Infantino and thanked him for his support for African football over the years.Ideally, Uefa would force an emergency meeting of the Fifa Council, to provide what it would consider to be a true chance to hold Infantino to account.But getting the necessary 19 of 36 confederation and football association heads to support it has proven to be exceptionally difficult. Uefa has also kept on the table the option of a vote of no confidence, which it can trigger via an extraordinary congress any time it wishes. However, it would need a majority of Fifa's 211 member associations - 106 votes - to pass the motion. It would be a de facto presidential election without a second candidate. If Uefa does not think it can get to 106, which looks a stretch, then there is little point in triggering the vote. The other option is to try to find a unity candidate to stand against Infantino in the election next March. The favourite would be Concacaf president Victor Montagliani. Any option which takes time gives Infantino space to build bridges, and with Fifa due to announce new funding to member associations by the end of the year he could dangle another carrot for his re-election.  Unless Uefa sticks by the nuclear option - and goes through with its threat of a boycott.This has issues, and it is not a lever you can pull very often, otherwise it gives the impression of riding roughshod over the rest of the world.It is one thing to use it to jettison the FFE proposal, another entirely to effectively dethrone the president with it. Uefa's stance will soon be tested, with the Fifa Women's U20s World Cup kicking off in Poland on 5 September. Six European countries are due to take part, including England. Some at the European confederation claim Wednesday's statement shows exactly why the beleaguered president must step down.The feeling within Uefa is that the statement was far from representative of the entire world governing body, and that there has been a lack of consultation with the council or membership.There is also a view that Infantino is trying to swerve personal responsibility by sharing out the blame for the aborted proposals, and that he alone should have apologised - rather than issue his expression of regret alongside his deputy Grafstrom.In stark contrast, within Fifa, the view from one Infantino loyalist is that the outcry, especially in Europe, is bordering on "hysteria", and fails to acknowledge the legitimacy he has globally.By clinging to power, Infantino has mounted the start of an attempted fightback. But it could yet fuel the revolt against him, both from outside and within Fifa. And it looks increasingly likely his opponents will have to identity the rival candidate that could challenge him at next year's presidential election.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Uefa says Fifa's backing of its president 'changes nothing'

title: Wales wildfires could see nature take centuries to recover - environmentalists
description: Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, PATRICK O'NEILLImage caption, A fire in the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd started on the Harlech side of
body: Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, PATRICK O'NEILLImage caption, A fire in the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd started on the Harlech side of the range, before spreading towards TrawsfynyddSlide 1 of 6, An aerial photo of the vast Rhinogydd mountain area. It shows a large mountain scorched by fire., A fire in the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd started on the Harlech side of the range, before spreading towards TrawsfynyddIt could be hundreds of years before habitats destroyed by wildfires in Wales recover, an environment watchdog has said.Nick Thomas, from Natural Resources Wales (NRW), said if soil had been incinerated in upland areas rich in peat, which grows at about a millimetre a year, it could take centuries for the vegetation to come back.He expects 2026 to be the worst year Wales has ever experienced.As well as damage to natural habitats and animal life, Thomas warned loss of soil could increase flood risks, because it no longer acted as a "sponge" holding water on high ground.Wales has witnessed huge wildfires this summer, including one major incident and the evacuation of a village in Conwy county.In the Rhinogydd mountain range in Gwynedd, which is home to a National Nature Reserve and a Special Area of Conservation, a blaze burned for nearly two weeks and affected over 2,000 acres.Both fires were visible from space.Meanwhile, a fire in Blaenavon, Torfaen, could be smelt as far away as Cardiff. Although fewer wildfires were reported in the second half of July in England and Wales compared with 2025, Thomas said: "This year seems to have been worse, I would say, than any of the ones I can remember."I would expect this to probably be the worst year for wildfires perhaps we've ever had."While some areas will recover quite quickly - potentially within a couple of years - he said: "It all depends on how deep the fire goes."If a fire burns into the soil and incinerates the soil... then you've lost hundreds of years worth of soil."So it's going to take hundreds of years really for that vegetation to come back in a similar way to what it was."The Pensychnant reserve is supported by volunteers who help preserve and run the centre, including Gwyndaf Pritchard, from Dwygyfylchi.He said it had been a special place for the community and that the loss of wildlife had been "tragic"."We've talked about it for years and years, but now climate change is here and we have to start to respect the countryside and we have to be in a position to actually stop these fires happening again," he said.Evie Roberts, a silversmith who teaches jewellery-making at the centre, said people needed to be educated about the dangers of discarding bottles or cigarettes, which could cause fires."Your actions can have devastating effects and I think that education for people is vital to stop this," she said."There's a new fire every week at the moment, and there's so much of our land damaged."

schema.headline: Wales wildfires could see nature take centuries to recover - environmentalists

title: Who will exit Chelsea? How Blues could cut 41-man squad
description: Chelsea are in the familiar position of having a large number of players on their books, with 41 senior players and only 25 days remaining in the tran
body: Chelsea are in the familiar position of having a large number of players on their books, with 41 senior players and only 25 days remaining in the transfer window to resolve the situation.With no European football this campaign, new boss Xabi Alonso is keen to significantly reduce his squad - with a number of players either available for sale or on loan.While the Blues can effectively register as many players as they want, despite the Premier League's 25-man squad rule - with under-21 and homegrown regulations covering the vast majority of players on their books - the Spaniard knows having players not involved cannot be good for squad harmony.But, even to get the squad down to a more manageable 25 senior players, Chelsea will need to offload 16 players by the start of September. The Blues have had players stranded in a 'bomb squad' in the past, like Raheem Sterling and Axel Disasi last season. That practice has since been outlawed by Fifa, increasing the importance of drastically reducing the squad.Had Chelsea qualified for Europe they would have been at risk of being unable to register certain players, as was the case during their 2024-25 Conference League-winning campaign. They are also bound by a Uefa settlement agreement for three more seasons, but European football's governing body has acknowledged they have made efforts to improve their finances. The Blues are accustomed to this level of player trading and are boosted by the fact they have largely built Alonso's squad through the signings of Morgan Rogers, Marco Palestra, Danny Welbeck, Jordan Henderson and Maxence Lacroix, with full-back Pep Chavarria close to joining from Rayo Vallecano.The size of the squad is an issue that needs addressing though. On Wednesday, they had 21 substitutes for their 1-0 defeat by Juventus in Hong Kong. Just five were academy players.Chelsea were keen to carry a large squad into the final few days of their Asian tour. They face AC Milan in Indonesia on Saturday before taking on Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta'zim on Sunday and will likely field two different XIs.But, it remains a remarkable number given both Cole Palmer and Levi Colwill were absent from the midweek match because of knocks sustained in the previous friendly, and striker Emmanuel Emegha is continuing his rehabilitation from a hamstring injury at the training ground.There are also five players not even training with the first team: Benoit Badiashile, Axel Disasi, Marc Guiu, David Datro Fofana and Caleb Wiley. They are all available either for permanent or loan moves.Seven players remain on holiday until next week having featured in the latter stages of the World Cup: Enzo Fernandez, Reece James, Rogers, Henderson, Lacroix, Valentin Barco and Malo Gusto.Defender Trevoh Chalobah is close to joining Como for £31m, including add-ons, while goalkeeper Filip Jorgensen is joining sister club Strasbourg on loan.Who is in and who is out?Chelsea are out of European football next season after finishing 10th in a campaign where Enzo Maresca left the club and Liam Rosenior was dismissed.Alonso has some difficult decisions ahead.His goalkeeping options appear set, with Robert Sanchez joined by exciting Belgian prospect Mike Penders, 21, following his impressive loan spell at French club Strasbourg, with with Teddy Sharman-Lowe likely to serve as the third-choice understudy.At full-back, club captain Reece James, also capable of playing in midfield, is joined on the right by Gusto and Palestra.Chelsea have put a £75m price tag on Gusto after Manchester City emerged as potential suitors.On the left, Chelsea have Jorrel Hato and are close to completing the £16.3m signing of Chavarria.At centre-back, Chelsea have nine players and Alonso has said the group needs reducing to "four or five".Disasi and Badiashile are available for sale, while Mamadou Sarr is expected to depart on loan. That would leave new signing Lacroix competing with Levi Colwill, Josh Acheampong, Wesley Fofana and Tosin Adarabioyo.It remains unclear what will happen with Argentina Under-20 international Aaron Anselmino, although another loan move appears likely having spent last term with Borussia Dortmund and Strasbourg.In midfield Chelsea have put a £120m price tag on Fernandez, who is exploring his options, although the club would also be happy to keep him.He is joined by fellow key central midfielder Moises Caicedo, fit-again Romeo Lavia, new signing Barco, who can play a number of positions in that area, Henderson and Dario Essugo.Essugo, 21, was previously told he would be staying but is open to a loan move because of his need for regular football after an injury-hit campaign.In attack, the shock return of Mykhailo Mudryk is another situation Chelsea must manage.The club insist all options remain open and are assessing his fitness following his return after 20 months out, because of a suspension relating to a positive test for the banned substance meldonium.Jamie Gittens is another option on the left wing, while Pedro Neto and new arrival Geovany Quenda are primarily right-sided players. Cole Palmer and Rogers are the two number 10s.Chelsea would also like to have three strikers going into next season. Alongside Joao Pedro and summer signing Welbeck, one further forward is likely to remain in the squad.That looks likely to be Emegha, although there remains uncertainty given Chelsea also have Nicolas Jackson and Liam Delap on their books.There is some overlap but, from information gathered by BBC Sport to date, this is the best projection of what Chelsea's squad could look like.Projected Chelsea squad: Sanchez, Penders, Sharman-Lowe, James, Palestra, Tosin, Fofana, Lacroix, Acheampong, Colwill, Hato, Chavarria, Caicedo, Fernandez, Barco, Lavia, Henderson, Quenda, Neto, Palmer, Estevao, Rogers, Gittens, Emegha, Joao Pedro, Welbeck.Available for loan: Guiu, Wiley, Kellyman, Mheuka, Walsh, Kavuma-McQueen, Kendry Paez.Available for sale/uncertain futures, with desired fees for some players in brackets: Badiashile (£30m), Disasi (£25m), Guiu (£25m), Datro Fofana, Delap, Jackson (£65m), Slonina, Gusto (£75m), Fernandez (£120m), Emegha, Neto, Essugo.Why Chelsea stockpile talentChelsea have been stockpiling players for more than a decade, dating back to former owner Roman Abramovich's reign.Under Abramovich, they had as many as 42 players out on loan before Fifa introduced limits designed to curb the practice.However, since Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital took charge in 2022 Chelsea have acquired Strasbourg, adding to the growing number of multi-club ownership models across Europe.They also embarked on a strategy of signing younger players on lower wages, who can be moved in and out as required.Among those signings was midfielder Andrey Santos, who arrived for £12m after a season in Brazil's second division before being sold to Manchester United for £50m.Chelsea have spent £1.8bn on acquiring talent since BlueCo took over the club four years ago, comfortably more than any other club in Europe.However, they have also raised nearly £1bn through player sales, including a Premier League record £300m, again the highest figure in Europe during that period.Chelsea are expected to make a similar number of sales this summer, with Chalobah's move to Como taking their total beyond £150m and Alejandro Garnacho's loan move to Aston Villa including an obligation to buy set to be worth about £40m next summer.They have the lowest revenues among the traditional 'big six' clubs. That is largely because of the size of Stamford Bridge, commercial underperformance, a kit deal with Adidas that has not kept pace with rivals, the absence of a front-of-shirt sponsor and missing out on Champions League football in three of the past four seasons.It is player trading that makes up much of that shortfall, in much the same way as it does for Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth, albeit with loftier ambitions of winning trophies and qualifying for the Champions League.

schema.headline: Who will exit Chelsea? How Blues could cut 41-man squad
